blocks.text: The Court Yard of a State Prison. In the back ground the principal gate, and a high rampart wall, over which trees are seen branching out. In the gate, which is closed, there is a little door for foot-passengers. At the side of the gate is the gate-keeper’s lodge. The side scenes on the left (of the spectators) present the dwelling of the prisoners. All the windows are grated; and the doors, which are marked with numbers, are strongly bolted. At the foremost wing (a side scene) is the door of the residence of the Turnkey. On the right stand trees, inclosed within iron railings; which together with a garden gate, point out the entrance to the castle garden.

Marceline is seen ironing linen at her door; near her stands the fire-pan in which she heats her irons. Jacquino, who keeps closer to the door, opens it to several persons, who present him with parcels, or packets of letters; he carries them into his little room.
Now, my little treasure, we are alone, now we may chat in confidence.
Surely it cannot be so important, I dare not tarry at my work.
A little word, you cross one, you!
If you look so cross, I won’t say a word.
If you won’t please me, I’ll stop my ears altogether.
Never more shall I be at rest.
I will then leave you alone! I have chosen a wife, and you know it’s yourself.
And if I got your consent, what mean you?
And in a few weeks we might—
Why we are then a pair.
This is charming. You are already settling the time, and I am released at last.
Oh, I was so happily pleased, but I am always losing the catch.
My hours last now for ever, I know this wretched one is his own torment; I pity him. But Fidelio is my choice, and to love him my greatest delight!
Where was I? She does not look upon me.
When shall you give your consent, and why not to-day?
You are really as hard as a stone.
Alas, he embitters my life, now, to-morrow, and always no!
I really must be hard with him.
And all desires, entreaties, are in vain!
And will you ever be stubborn? What say you?
Your sight even you forbid me?
Also this? You promised me so often. Oh, the deuce! that eternal knocking.
You may go, or stay here. I promised you? No, not so quick.
And who knows if I did not succeed.
That was a welcome sound. I was frightened to death.
Now, if I haven’t opened this door already two hundred times to-day, my name is not Casper Eustach Jacquino.
At last we can chat again.
It is no fancy of mine that I can no longer love him as formerly.
To the person who has been knocking, shutting the door after him hastily
I’ll take care of it. All’s right.
Now I hope nobody will interrupt us.
Well, he may wait a little; but to return to our love matters.
Get ye gone; father’s inquiry will be after Fidelio.
Ay, indeed; then all haste is not enough.
stay you here, my love; in two minutes I am again with you.

Poor Jacquino! I almost pity him. The compassion I feel for him still enhances my love for Fidelio. I really believe that Fidelio is very fond of me too; and if I knew my father’s mind, my happiness might soon be complete.

lines: Oh, how happy would I be, if in wedlock united with thee,
And my husband I can call thee;
But silence becomes best a maiden who’s in love, they say.
But I need not blush at a kind and heartfelt kiss,
Where nought on earth disturbs the hope that fills my breast.
Oh what delight! what bliss is mine!
How happy I! each morn fresh joy does bring,
With fond embrace in union blest, each other’s heart we tell.
All care we from our door bid fly, the labor o’er, fair night approaches,
And sweet rest to us does bring.
Oh what delight, etc.

blocks.text: Good day, Marceline! So Fidelio is not yet come back.
The hour approaches when I must take the letters to the governor, which Fidelio was to call for. I begin to grow rather impatient.
Runs alertly to unlock the door.
He has surely been detained at the smith’s.
There he is! there he is!

The above. Leonora carrying on her back a large basket, with provisions, and on her arms fetters, which on coming in she deposits in the gatekeeper’s room. A tin-plate box hangs from her side by a ribbon.
How he is laden! Good heaven! his poor forehead!
She takes her handkerchief, and endeavors to wipe Leonora’s brow.
He assists her, together with Marceline, to take the basket from her back.
Well, it was worth while to run so fast to let the fellow in.
He enters his little room, but returns soon pretending to be busily engaged, when, in reality, he is trying to watch the others.
Poor Fidelio! This time thou hast indeed burdened thyself too much.
Advancing by the side, and wiping her face and brow.
I must confess I am a little fatigued.
What’s the amount of it altogether?
About twelve piastres;—here is the exact account.

Well done. Zounds; there are articles amongst it of which twice the prime cost may be got. Thou art a sharp lad! I scarcely can conceive how you manage matters so cleverly. You buy every thing cheaper than I do. During the six months I have let it over to you to buy the provisions, you have gained more than I have in a whole year!
Ah! it’s evident the rogue gives himself all this trouble for the sake of my Marceline.
I endeavor to do all in my power.
Yes, yes, you are a worthy lad. It is impossible to be more zealous or more skillful. Now, you are getting every day more in my favor, and be assured a reward will not be wanted.
While speaking the last words, he glances alternately at Leonora and Marceline.
Oh, don’t think I fulfill my duty merely for the sake of reward.
Thinkest thou I could not look into thy heart?

He is pleased with the increasing confusion of Leonora; he then steps aside to look at the fetters. Whilst Rocquo is commending Leonora, Marceline manifests the greatest interest, and gazes on her with continually increasing emotion.

lines: What rapture do I feel, my heart is oppressed!
He loves me it’s clear, I shall be happy.
Alas, what danger! and hope is but vain!
She loves me, what pain.
She loves him, it’s clear; yes, girl, he is thine,
A good young couple; they shall be happy.
My hair stands on end, her father consents;
I don’t know how I am, nor what to do.

blocks.text: Hark, Fidelio! Tho’ I don’t know how and where thou wert born, and if you haven’t had any father at all, yet I know what I am about; I make you my son-in-law.

As soon as the governor has set out for Seville we have more leisure; you know he goes there every month to give account of all that occurs in the prison. In a few days he must be off again. The day after his departure I give you to each other—on that you may depend.
The day after his departure; that’s acting very prudently, dear father.
Before much puzzled, but now assuming a joyful air.
Oh! what a new and cruel embarrassment is here!
Now, my children! you love each other dearly, do you not? but that’s not all that is required to make marriage happy; there is likewise needed.

lines: If we have no money, love cannot comfort bring,
Sadly life drags on, and sorrow follows.
But when the coin jingles in the pockets,
Then fate is our prisoner.
Yes, gold brings love and power,
And all our wishes fills.
Happiness is the slave of gold;
Oh what a precious thing is gold!
Nought with nought united, what remains?
At dinner sweet love, and after dinner hunger;
May fate smile upon you and bless your endeavors.
Arm in arm, plenty of money in the purse;
Many a year may you thus live.
Yes, happiness is subservient to gold; oh, what a precious thing is gold!

blocks.text: You can easily say so, Mr. Rocquo; yet in truth now there is something else which would not be less precious to me; but I observe with sorrow that with all my endeavors I cannot obtain it.

Your confidence. Pardon the reproach; but frequently do I see you return from the subterraneous vaults of this castle, quite out of breath and spent with fatigue. Why don’t you allow me to accompany you thither? It would quite delight me if I could assist your duties, and share your toils.
But you know that I have the strictest order not to admit any one whatever to the state prisoners.
But there are by far too many in this fortress; you work and weary yourself to death, dear father.
She is in the right, Mr. Rocquo; a man should certainly fulfill his duty;
but methinks it is but justice we spare ourselves for those that belong to us, and love us.
Pressing Rocquo’s other hand to her bosom.
A good man must endeavor to preserve himself for his children’s sake.
Looks at them both much affected.
Yes, you are in the right. The heavy labor would in the end become too much for me. The governor is indeed very severe, but yet he must permit that I take you with me into the secret dungeons.
Leonora manifests a powerful feeling of joy.
There is, however, one dungeon, into which I shall never be able to take you though I am perfectly confident of you.
Probably where the prisoner is confined of whom you have already sometimes spoken, father.
I believe it is a long time ago since he was taken.
Two years! say you. He must be a great criminal.
Or he must have great enemies—that means nearly the same thing.
And could you never learn where he comes from and what is his name?
Often, indeed, has he wished to speak with me about all that.
But for folks like us it is best to know as few secrets as possible, therefore I have never listened to him. I might have gossiped to my injury, without doing him any good.
Well, poor fellow, he will not much longer plague me, he cannot last a very long while.
Oh, dear father! do not take Fidelio to him, this sight he could not bear.
Why not? I have courage and nerve enough.

Bravo, my son, bravo! Ah! if I were to tell you how I had to struggle with my heart at the first, in my situation; yet I was quite a different fellow, to what you are, with your fair skin and white hands.

lines: Good, my son, good! be ever of good cheer,
Then will you succeed. The heart gets hardened
When often in contact with horrible scenes.
I have courage; with calmness
Will I venture down, for high reward.
Love will endure high sufferings also.
Thy good heart will suffer
Woefully in those dread vaults; but the joys of love
Await thee in return, and happiness will be thine.
Thy fortune is in thy own hands, my lad.
I confide in God and in right.
You may espy in my eyes, that not small is love’s power.
Yes, yes, we shall be happy.
To-day the governor consents that you share my duty.
You destroy my rest if you delay till to-morrow.
Good father, intreat him to-day; the sooner is our union.
I shall soon go down to my grave.
A long time I have been a prey to woe.
I need help, and it’s true.
A ray of hope fills me.
Ah, good father, what think you?
Long, long you’ll be our friend and consoler.
Only be prudent, and all goes well;
Gratified your wishes are.
Oh, have courage; oh, what ardor!
Oh, what a deep feeling!
You are so good, you inspire me with courage,
Fulfilled is my desire.
Shake hands and be united.
I have given my sacred pledge—
Ah! what bitter tears it cost me.
A lasting tie, with hand and heart—
Oh! sweet and welcome tears.
In sweet tears of joy.
It costs bitter tears.
Oh! sweet, sweet tears.

blocks.text: But now it’s time that I carry the papers to the governor.
give them me, Fidelio, and then depart.
Leonora takes the tin-plate box which is suspended by a ribbon, gives it to Rocquo, and goes away with Marceline into the house.
During the March the principal gate opens from without; Officers with a detachment enter, then Pizarro. The gate is again closed.
Three guards on the rampart, six day and night on the drawbridge, the same number on the side of the garden, and whosoever comes near is immediately brought before me.
Taking the papers out of a box.
Opens the papers, and goes through them.
Ever commands and reprimands. I should never have done were I to pay attention to all this. What do I see? I fancy I know this writing; let’s see.
He opens the letter, advancing a step. Rocquo and the guards step back—he reads.

“I inform you what the minister has learned; that among the state prisoners there under your charge, several are victims of arbitrary power; he departs to-morrow to surprise you with an examination. Be on your guard, and endeavor to keep yourself right.”
Ha! if he should discover that I have this Florestan lying here in chains, whom he has long ago thought to be dead! One bold deed can and must disperse all my anxieties.

lines: Ah, what a moment! Yes, I’ll be revenged.
Thy fate calls! Yes, his heart I pierce.
Oh, joy! high delight! Already crouched in dust was I,
A prey to base mockery stretched to the ground,
But now mine it is to kill him that would have killed me.
In his last hour, the steel in his bosom.
Yes, I cry aloud in his ear—
Triumph! mine is the victory!

blocks.text: He speaks of death and vengeance. Watch carefully.
And mind well on your rounds—it must be important.
He leads the captain forward and speaks softly to him.
Ascend the tower together with a trumpeter. Look with the greatest attention towards the high road to Seville.
As soon as you perceive a carriage surrounded with riders, let me instantly hear a signal. You understand, instantly? I expect the greatest punctuality. With your head you answer for it.
Looks at him attentively for a short time
I must endeavor to win him over; without his help I cannot execute my design. Come, approach!
Now, old friend, haste! your fortune’s made. A man of riches you.
There, this is only to commence with.
Oh, quick, ah, say, in what can I serve you?
Thou art of old blood, of undaunted courage from long service.
Listen. You tremble; are you a man? We must delay no longer, on account of the state; quick, a subject so bad must be got rid of.
He must live no longer, or I’m undone. Ha! Pizzarro in fears should live! No! you die. I stand.
My frame is trembling! how could I bear it? No; his life I’ll not take, let happen what may. Sir, to kill I am not in duty bound.
I’ll do it myself if your courage fails. Only quick, haste down to the man you know.
Who scarcely lives the semblance of a shadow?
Yes, to him, to him down. I at short distance wait. And in the cistern a grave prepare, quick, for him.
You give a signal; and I in disguise quick in the dungeon descend.
One blow, and he is dumb.
Famishing in chains his sufferings are great; to kill him is to save him, and mine is rest.
Exit Pizzarro towards the garden, Rocquo follows him.
Leonora appears in great agitation from the opposite side; she observes those that go away with increasing anxiety.

lines: Monster! Whither in thy haste? what design breeds thy rage?
Nor pity’s call, nor humanity’s voice, nought moves thy tiger mind.
Yet I see the storm of passion within thy soul does rage;
But a ray of hope on heaven’s face I still perceive;
It brings me calm, restores my soul;
In fond recollection of past happiness my heart now beats anew.
Sweet hope forsake not this lingering heart!
Oh! let a ray of joy console my sorrowing love.
See, my bosom beats, I hesitate not—
Yes, a wife devout—I—fresh vigor bring.

blocks.text: Marceline, from the house, Jacquino follows her.
Not a word, not a syllable. I will hear nothing more of your silly love tales, and that’s enough.

Who would have said this, when I earnestly fell in love with you? Then I was dear Jacquino; dear here, and dear there. Dear Jacquino puts the irons to the fire, dear Jacquino folds up the linen, he takes the parcels to the prisoners; in short, must do all that a maiden asks of an honorable lad; but since this Fidelio—
I don’t deny I was good to you; but look, I’m open hearted. It was not love. Fidelio is more endearing; I find a great harmony between him and me.
An harmony with such a vagabond, who comes from God knows where; whom your father out of mere charity, received at the gate, and who—
Who is poor and forsaken, and whom I shall as yet marry.
Believe you I shall suffer that? It will not take place in my presence, or see I might play you a trick.
The former, Rocquo, Leonora, from the garden.
Ah, father, he ever will tease me?
He wants me to marry him, to love him, and I—
Silence! Surely, my only daughter, whom I have brought up with such care to her sixteenth year,
and all for this fine gentleman?
No, friend Jacquino, other thoughts fill my mind.

Now end we this conversation. Rocquo, I begged of you many times to suffer the poor prisoners, those that dwell above ground to walk about in the free air of the garden. You promised it me, but continually defer it. To-day the weather is fine; the governor does not come here at this time.
Oh, yes; I entreat with him!
My dear children, without the permission of the governor?
But you were speaking to him for a long time; perhaps you are to do him a favor, and then he will not be so particular.
A favor? You are in the right, Marceline! On this risk I may venture it. Well, then, Jacquino and Fidelio, go and open the minor cells, and I will go to Pizzarro, and detain him, at the same time,
I’ll speak to him for your best!
Exit Rocquo. Leonora and Jacquino open the gates of the prison; they retire with Marceline in the background, and observe, with sympathy, the prisoners, who shortly make their appearance.

lines: Oh, what enjoyment to breathe the fresh air of heaven!
Here only is to live; the dungeon is a tomb.
Let us trust in heaven with confidence!
Hope softly whispers—“You will be free, you will have peace.”
O Heaven! Deliverance! what a blessing! Oh, liberty returnest thou?
Speak softly—restrain yourselves! We are watched by eyes and ears.
Speak softly—restrain yourselves! We are watched by eyes and ears.

blocks.text: Now speak, how did you succeed?

Well! very well! I composed my mind and mentioned every thing. And, would you believe it? That he gave the answer? He allows the marriage, and that you assist me. This very day you shall go with me to the dungeons.
I can see your joy. Only another moment and we both do go.
Down to that man whom for weeks past I have continually diminished the food.
We—yes, we must free him. In one hour your lips are closed—He must be in his grave.
No, no, my fine fellow, never fear—Rocquo is no murderer. The governor himself comes down—we only dig the grave.
Perhaps to dig the grave of the husband, oh! what can be more horrible?
I dare not nourish him; in the grave he finds rest. We must proceed to work. You must help and accompany me. The goaler’s bread is hard.
In the old cistern, with ease we dig the grave, believe me I don’t like it, and you seem to shudder too.
I’m quite prepared, confide in me!
I willingly had spar’d you this. But, all alone, the work’s too much.
No, you remain here: I go alone.
I must see him, the wretched man, even on my own peril.
Then delay we no longer; we follow duty’s call.
Marceline, and Jacquino, rushing in out of breath.
Filled with rage, Pizzarro follows my steps threatening you.
Another word more! speak! knows he then?
The officer told him of the new indulgence the prisoners have.
You know how he rages, and are aware of his fury.
How my heart beats! my soul is all in arms.
My heart rejoices, let the tyrant rave.
Pizzarro, two officers, Guards: the above.
Audacious old man! what rights are you criminally assuming?
Does it become the hireling servant to deliver the prisoners?
The coming of spring, the serene ray of the sun, besides—consider—
—Our gracious king’s birthday—we celebrate in this manner.
The one below dies; but suffer the others an happy hour in the free air; reserve your fury for him alone.
Then hasten to dig his grave; here all must be quiet. Shut up again the prisoners, and never be so daring again.
Farewell, warm ray of the sun, soon thou vanishest again. Night breaks upon us, and never to behold again the morn.
Now, Rocquo, tarry no longer, descend into the dungeon.
Return not till accomplished is my will.
No, Sir, no, I tarry no longer, I hasten down.
My limbs tremble; oh, severe and dread duty!
You hear the word—then linger here no longer. Return into the prison; fear overpowers me! Does no judgment overtake this wicked man?
We hastened to behold the light of day—But part again in sorrow. Alas, no cheering ray of joy or hope within these melancholy walls does dwell.
You hear the word, tarry no longer, return into the prison!
Aside, looking upon Rocquo and Leonora
Ah, you are meditating; I wish I knew what each does mean.
